sections.title: Explain oxygen and carbon dioxide loss from leaves
paragraphs: Photosynthesis produces oxygen, which can be a waste product when more is made than the plant uses. Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide. These gases can leave a leaf by diffusion through stomata down their own concentration gradients.

Plants both photosynthesise and respire. Some oxygen made in photosynthesis can be used in respiration, and some respiratory carbon dioxide can be used in photosynthesis. The net gas exchange depends on the balance of the processes.

In bright conditions photosynthesis may exceed respiration, giving net oxygen release and carbon dioxide uptake. In darkness photosynthesis stops but respiration continues, giving net carbon dioxide release. Do not say that plant respiration occurs only at night.

example.question: Why can a photosynthesising leaf still make carbon dioxide internally?
steps: Its living cells continue respiration.
Photosynthesis can use that carbon dioxide at the same time.
Net outside exchange shows the balance, not the absence of one internal process.
example.explanation: Identify the source process and then the direction supported by the gas gradient.

practice.question: Which process produces oxygen as a metabolic by-product?
practice.explanation: Identify the source process and then the direction supported by the gas gradient.

commonMistakes: Do not claim plants respire only in darkness or always lose both gases simultaneously.

sections.title: Distinguish excretion from egestion
paragraphs: Excretion removes metabolic waste and excess substances from the body. Lungs remove carbon dioxide produced by respiration and also lose water vapour. Kidneys remove urea, excess water and ions in urine.
The skin loses water and salts in sweat, with small amounts of urea. Sweating is especially important for temperature regulation; it is not the main route removing urea compared with the kidneys.

Egestion removes undigested material from the alimentary canal as faeces. This is distinct from removing metabolic waste made by cells. Do not call every substance leaving the body a product of excretion.

example.question: Classify carbon dioxide exhaled from lungs and undigested fibre leaving in faeces.
steps: Cell respiration makes carbon dioxide: its removal is excretion.
Undigested fibre remains in the gut: its removal is egestion.
Use origin as well as the exit route.
example.explanation: A waste classification depends on where the material came from.

practice.question: Which organ provides the principal urinary route for urea removal?
practice.explanation: A waste classification depends on where the material came from.

commonMistakes: Do not say the lungs excrete oxygen as the main respiratory waste or confuse faeces with urine.

sections.title: Separate waste removal from water balance
paragraphs: Kidneys excrete metabolic wastes such as urea from blood and regulate the balance of water and dissolved ions. Urea is formed in the liver during processing of excess amino acids; kidneys remove it rather than being its main site of production.

Osmoregulation controls body water balance so cells are not exposed to uncontrolled osmotic changes. The kidneys adjust how much water and other substances remain in urine while returning needed material to blood.

Filtration is followed by selective processing. It would be wasteful to excrete every molecule entering the filtrate: glucose is useful, and much of the water is needed. Excretion and regulation are related but distinct kidney roles.

example.question: Why does “the kidney filters out all useful water” misdescribe its function?
steps: Water enters filtrate with small solutes.
Much is returned to blood, with the final amount regulated.
Urine removes waste while avoiding unnecessary loss of needed material.
example.explanation: Explain both removal of waste and controlled retention of needed substances.

practice.question: Does osmoregulation mean making urine contain no water?
practice.answer: No. It means regulating water balance, not eliminating water from urine.
practice.explanation: Explain both removal of waste and controlled retention of needed substances.

commonMistakes: Do not say kidneys create the urea they remove or permanently discard all filtered substances.

sections.title: Trace urine through the urinary system
paragraphs: The kidneys form urine. Each ureter carries urine from a kidney to the bladder, which stores it temporarily. The urethra carries urine from the bladder to outside the body.

Blood reaches a kidney through a renal artery and returns through a renal vein. Those vessels carry blood, whereas ureters and the urethra carry urine. Their similar names do not indicate identical functions.
The bladder stores urine; it does not perform the initial blood filtration. Keep formation, transport, storage and release as separate stages.

example.question: Put kidney, urethra, bladder and ureter in the urine route.
steps: Kidney → ureter → bladder → urethra → outside.
Renal blood vessels belong to a separate blood route.
The two ureters enter the bladder; the urethra leaves it.
example.explanation: Name each stage and state what fluid moves through it.

practice.question: Which tube connects a kidney to the bladder?
practice.explanation: Name each stage and state what fluid moves through it.

commonMistakes: Do not swap ureter and urethra or call the bladder a blood filter.

sections.title: Locate the parts of a nephron
paragraphs: A nephron is a microscopic kidney processing unit. The glomerulus is a capillary knot surrounded by Bowman’s capsule. Blood stays inside the capillaries while filtrate enters the capsule space.

Filtrate travels from Bowman’s capsule to the proximal convoluted tubule, around the loop of Henle and through the distal convoluted tubule towards a collecting duct. Convoluted means coiled; the loop descends and returns.

The capsule and convoluted tubules lie in the outer cortex. The loop extends into the medulla, and collecting ducts carry fluid towards the kidney’s drainage region. Blood vessels alongside the tubules receive reabsorbed material.
A collecting duct receives fluid from several nephrons. Calling it part of the taught nephron route does not mean one isolated duct serves only one nephron or that blood flows through its lumen.

example.question: Where is the first separation between blood and newly formed filtrate?
steps: At the glomerular filtration barrier into Bowman’s capsule.
Blood stays in the capillary route.
Filtrate enters the tubule route beginning at the capsule.
example.explanation: Follow the two fluids separately and locate their exchange stages.

practice.question: Does a renal vein directly empty into a collecting duct?
practice.answer: No. The renal vein carries blood; the collecting duct carries modified filtrate towards urine drainage.
practice.explanation: Follow the two fluids separately and locate their exchange stages.

commonMistakes: Do not draw one uninterrupted tube that mixes the blood route with the filtrate route.

diagram.alt: Original functional route chart: blood is filtered from the glomerulus into Bowman’s capsule; filtrate follows proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting duct. Glucose and water return from tubules to nearby blood capillaries. Routes are separate and not drawn anatomically.
diagram.caption: Original functional chart, not anatomy or scale. Filtration moves material into the tubule route; reabsorption returns selected material to blood.

sections.title: Explain pressure filtration at the glomerulus
paragraphs: Blood enters the glomerulus under pressure. The pressure drives water and sufficiently small dissolved substances across the filtration barrier into Bowman’s capsule. This is ultrafiltration, not a process that selects only wastes.

The barrier retains blood cells and most large plasma proteins in healthy blood. Water, glucose, urea and small ions can enter the filtrate. A useful molecule such as glucose can therefore be filtered along with waste.

The resulting filtrate is not identical to whole blood: it normally lacks blood cells and most large proteins. It is also not yet the final urine, because later reabsorption and other processing alter it.

example.question: Why can glucose be in the filtrate even though the body needs it?
steps: Glomerular filtration depends on the barrier and pressure, not whether a small molecule is useful.
Glucose can pass into the filtrate.
It can then be selectively reabsorbed downstream.
example.explanation: Separate pressure-driven entry from later selective recovery.

practice.question: Are red cells expected in normal glomerular filtrate?
practice.answer: No. They are retained by the intact filtration barrier.
practice.explanation: Separate pressure-driven entry from later selective recovery.

commonMistakes: Do not say only urea is filtered or that the capsule fills with whole blood.

sections.title: Compare blood, filtrate and urine
paragraphs: Blood contains plasma plus cells and platelets. Fresh glomerular filtrate contains water and small solutes such as glucose, urea and ions, but normally lacks cells and most large proteins.

As filtrate passes through tubules, useful glucose and much water are returned to blood. The final urine contains water, urea and ions; normally it contains no appreciable glucose under ordinary healthy conditions.

A concentration and a total mass are different quantities. A smaller volume can contain the same mass at a higher concentration. Do not infer that more urea was produced just because a urine sample is more concentrated.

example.question: Two constructed samples each contain 10 mg of urea. Their volumes are 5 cm³ and 10 cm³. Compare concentrations.
steps: First: 10 ÷ 5 = 2 mg/cm³.
Second: 10 ÷ 10 = 1 mg/cm³.
The first is twice as concentrated but both contain the same 10 mg mass. These are constructed examples, not patient results.
example.explanation: Compare the stage, the composition and the measured quantity.

practice.question: Is newly formed glomerular filtrate already identical to final urine?
practice.answer: No. Later selective reabsorption and regulation change its composition and volume.
practice.explanation: Compare the stage, the composition and the measured quantity.

commonMistakes: Do not confuse higher concentration with greater total waste mass or use a classroom sample to diagnose disease.

sections.title: Explain water reabsorption from collecting ducts
paragraphs: Water can pass from the collecting-duct fluid through the duct wall into surrounding tissue and then nearby blood capillaries. The net movement is by osmosis down a water-potential gradient.
The concentration of the surrounding medullary tissue helps provide the gradient. The amount reabsorbed also depends on collecting-duct water permeability, which is influenced by ADH.

Water is not actively pumped as water molecules, and reabsorption is not movement back into the stomach. It returns filtered material to the internal blood supply. Much water is also reabsorbed earlier along the tubule, so not all recovery occurs in the collecting duct.

example.question: Why does a more water-permeable collecting duct not alone prove water will move in any direction?
steps: Permeability allows movement but a water-potential difference sets the net direction.
In the normal concentrating pathway water moves from duct fluid towards surrounding tissue and blood.
State osmosis and the gradient rather than an unexplained water pump.
example.explanation: Explain both the available route and the gradient driving net water movement.

practice.question: Does ADH directly pump water molecules against their water-potential gradient?
practice.answer: No. It changes permeability; water moves by osmosis.
practice.explanation: Explain both the available route and the gradient driving net water movement.

commonMistakes: Do not call water reabsorption active transport or locate every reabsorption step only in the collecting duct.

sections.title: Explain selective glucose reabsorption
paragraphs: Glucose in fresh filtrate is useful for respiration, so the proximal convoluted tubule normally returns it to blood instead of losing it in urine. This is selective reabsorption because particular substances are recovered.

Tubule cells use transport proteins and energy-linked transport processes. At this level it can be described as active glucose reabsorption; more precisely, entry uses sodium–glucose cotransport driven by a gradient maintained using ATP. Water osmosis is a different process.

Under ordinary healthy conditions the filtered glucose load is within the tubule’s transport capacity, so essentially all is recovered. Capacity is finite; sufficiently high filtered loads or altered transport can leave glucose in urine. This qualification is not a diagnosis from a single sample.

example.question: Why is “glucose must be removed because it is waste” incorrect?
steps: Glucose supplies energy for respiration and is useful.
It is small enough to enter initial filtrate.
The proximal tubule selectively recovers it into blood.
example.explanation: Distinguish the reason for recovery from the transport mechanism.

practice.question: Does selective reabsorption mean that no glucose was ever filtered?
practice.answer: No. Filtration occurs first; reabsorption then returns glucose.
practice.explanation: Distinguish the reason for recovery from the transport mechanism.

commonMistakes: Do not explain glucose recovery as osmosis or say its transport capacity is unlimited.

sections.title: Trace ADH in water-balance control
paragraphs: When blood becomes too concentrated after water loss, receptors in the hypothalamus detect the change. ADH is made in the hypothalamus and stored and released by the posterior pituitary into blood.

More ADH increases the water permeability of collecting ducts, allowing more water-channel proteins at the relevant cell surface. More water returns to blood by osmosis, conserving water and producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine in the simplified comparison.

As blood concentration moves back towards the normal range, the stimulus for additional ADH release decreases. This is negative feedback: the response opposes the original change, rather than amplifying it indefinitely.

After excess water makes blood more dilute, less ADH is released, collecting ducts are less permeable and a larger volume of dilute urine can be produced. This is a comparison with other conditions held suitable; illness and other control signals can alter the result.

example.question: Trace the response to loss of body water in four linked steps.
steps: Blood becomes more concentrated and receptors detect the change.
More ADH is released into blood from the posterior pituitary.
Collecting ducts become more water-permeable, so more water is reabsorbed by osmosis.
The blood change is opposed and less, more concentrated urine is formed.
example.explanation: Use detection → hormone → permeability → reabsorption → feedback as a causal sequence.

practice.question: Is ADH made in the kidney?
practice.answer: No. It is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary; the kidney is a target.
practice.explanation: Use detection → hormone → permeability → reabsorption → feedback as a causal sequence.

commonMistakes: Do not reverse the ADH effect or confuse hormone production, release and target.

sections.title: Compare urine volume and concentration
paragraphs: Compare water balance before trying to memorise a urine label. Water loss tends to increase ADH and recovery of water into blood. Excess water tends to lower ADH and reduce the regulated recovery.

More recovered water generally means less remains in the urine, making it more concentrated relative to a suitable comparison. This does not mean ADH creates extra urea or that there is no water left.

A fair response explanation states what changed and keeps the direction consistent. Greater collecting-duct permeability, greater water reabsorption and a larger urine volume would contradict one another in the simple other-things-equal model.

example.question: Correct: “ADH rises, less water is reabsorbed, and the urine becomes dilute.”
steps: With more ADH, collecting-duct water permeability increases.
More water is reabsorbed into blood by osmosis.
Less water remains in urine, so its volume is lower and concentration higher in the comparison.
example.explanation: Follow the water rather than changing the causal direction mid-answer.

practice.question: Does concentrated urine necessarily contain more total urea than a dilute sample?
practice.answer: No. Concentration depends on mass divided by volume; the total mass must be checked separately.
practice.explanation: Follow the water rather than changing the causal direction mid-answer.

commonMistakes: Do not reverse volume and concentration or infer a universal hormone measurement from one urine appearance.

sections.title: State what remains for urinary excretion
paragraphs: Urine contains water, urea and dissolved ions. The amounts and concentrations vary as the kidneys regulate water and ion balance and remove metabolic waste.

Urea contains nitrogen originating from amino-acid processing in the liver. It is delivered in blood and removed into the urine route; it is not undigested food travelling from the stomach to the bladder.

Normal urine in the simplified healthy model has no appreciable glucose, blood cells or large plasma proteins. Do not turn this classroom comparison into an absolute statement covering all disease states or a diagnostic test.

example.question: A response lists water, urea and red cells as the required normal urine components. Repair it.
steps: Keep water and urea.
Replace red cells with dissolved ions.
Blood cells normally remain in the blood rather than crossing the intact filtration barrier.
example.explanation: Name the specified components and distinguish normal composition from every possible condition.

practice.question: Is urine pure urea with no water?
practice.answer: No. It is a solution containing water, urea and ions among other dissolved products.
practice.explanation: Name the specified components and distinguish normal composition from every possible condition.

commonMistakes: Do not equate urine with faeces, pure urea or unmodified filtrate.
